jobLabels.escape: switching your brain off for a while
jobLabels.soothe: quieting your head when feelings get loud
jobLabels.reassure: making sure nothing bad is happening without you
jobLabels.avoid: not starting the thing you're dreading

regulator.name: The Late-Night Regulator
regulator.quote: I can't be alone with my head at night, so I stay with the screen until I pass out.
regulator.read: Your screen isn't entertainment at night — it's a buffer between you and your own thoughts. It works, which is exactly the problem: it borrows the relief from tomorrow's sleep, and tomorrow keeps paying.
regulator.pull: Whatever fills silence — the platform matters less than the hour
regulator.job: Quieting the mind; avoiding being alone with thoughts before sleep
regulator.advice: The lever isn't willpower at midnight — it's a wind-down that does the soothing job some other way, built gradually, plus protecting the hour before bed like it's medical. Because it kind of is.

spiral.name: The Comparison Spiral
spiral.quote: I open it to see where I stand, and I leave feeling worse — then I open it again.
spiral.read: Scrolling stopped being entertainment somewhere along the way and became evaluation: of your body, your progress, your life. The feed sets the bar, you measure yourself against it, and checking feels compulsory even though it reliably hurts.
spiral.pull: Visual feeds with rankings, metrics, and an algorithm that learned what stings
spiral.job: Checking where you stand; seeking proof you're okay
spiral.advice: The comparison belief is the target, not the app. Retraining the feed helps fast; learning to catch the moment content becomes a verdict on you is the deeper work — and it's very learnable.

gamer.name: The Achievement-Escape Gamer
gamer.quote: The game is the only place I'm good at something.
gamer.read: This isn't laziness and it never was. The game gives you visible progress, earned respect, and control — usually exactly when school or work is making you feel behind and stupid. Avoiding the work makes it scarier, which makes the game more necessary. That loop is the whole machine.
gamer.pull: Ranked progress, visible mastery, a world where effort pays off
gamer.job: Feeling competent and in control; escaping the failure-feeling
gamer.advice: Shrinking the game without rebuilding offline competence fails every time. Start ridiculously small on the avoided thing (two-minute starts), and treat focus issues seriously — for this pattern, an ADHD conversation is often the unlock.

drifter.name: The Infinite Drifter
drifter.quote: I'm not choosing this. I just look up and an hour is gone.
drifter.read: There's no dramatic craving here — that's what makes it slippery. The feed fills every gap before you've decided anything, and the time disappears in transitions: after school, between tasks, before starting. Often it isn't even fun. It's just frictionless.
drifter.pull: Infinite feeds engineered to remove every stopping point
drifter.job: Filling gaps; dodging the friction of starting things
drifter.advice: Don't fight it with willpower — fight it with architecture. Friction at the open (app position, grayscale, an intention prompt) plus an honest answer to one question: what do you actually want the reclaimed time for? Drift needs a destination to lose to.

checker.name: The Tethered Checker
checker.quote: If I don't check, I might already be left out and not know it.
checker.read: Your phone has become a social smoke detector. Every check buys a few minutes of “nothing bad is happening,” and every check teaches your brain that checking is what kept you safe. That's why it's getting more frequent, not less — reassurance is the most renewable anxiety fuel there is.
checker.pull: Streaks, read receipts, group chats — places where absence is visible
checker.job: Reassurance; confirming you're not being left out
checker.advice: This responds to the same approach as other reassurance loops: graduated delays (check in 10 minutes, then 20), letting the anxiety crest and fall without the check. It spikes before it settles. It settles.

socializer.name: The Safer-Online Socializer
socializer.quote: Online is where people make sense.
socializer.read: Your online world isn't fake — the friendships, the standing, the being-known are real. It's also where social risk goes to zero, and the longer offline stays unpracticed, the more impossible it feels. The community is both your asset and your hiding place, and both halves are true at once.
socializer.pull: Communities with identity, belonging, and no eye contact required
socializer.advice: Nobody should ask you to amputate your community. The move is bridging: take one thing that's true about you online — the humor, the expertise, the role — and find it one small offline outlet. Expansion, not exile.

shame.name: The Shame Cycle
shame.quote: The relief lasts minutes. The shame lasts longer. The shame brings me back.
shame.read: This pattern runs on a closed loop: stress or emptiness builds, the content delivers relief, the aftermath delivers shame, and shame is itself uncomfortable enough to restart the cycle. The secrecy adds weight. None of this makes you broken — it makes the loop well-built.
shame.job: Fast relief from stress, loneliness, or pressure
shame.advice: The target is the cycle, not your character. Shame is the loop's fuel — which is why white-knuckle promises fail and a non-judgmental approach (ideally with a professional who treats compulsive patterns) actually works. This is more common and more treatable than the secrecy lets you believe.

confidant.name: The Synthetic Confidant
confidant.quote: It's always awake, it never judges, and it never leaves.
confidant.read: You've found something that listens better than most people do — endlessly patient, always available, zero risk. The catch is quiet: every need it meets is a need that stops pushing you toward people, and human connection only gets easier with reps.
confidant.pull: An always-on companion with infinite patience
confidant.job: Being understood without judgment or risk
confidant.advice: Keep what works — the processing, the rehearsal space. But pick one thing per week that you told the AI and tell a human instead. The goal isn't quitting the tool; it's making sure it stays a bridge and not a destination.

outrage.name: The Outrage Loop
outrage.quote: It makes me furious. I check it constantly.
outrage.read: Outrage is stimulation with a moral alibi. The threads and feeds give you certainty, sides, and the most awake feeling in your day — then you leave more activated than you arrived, and the activation leaks onto the people around you. And you go back, because flat feels worse than angry.
outrage.pull: Conflict, takes, and rabbit holes that never resolve
outrage.job: Stimulation and certainty in an uncertain feed
outrage.advice: The need for intensity is legitimate — the diet is the problem. Replacement stimulation (real exertion, real competition, real stakes) plus a hard look at which sources exist purely to keep you lit. You're not the customer there; you're the product.

light_grip.label: Light grip
light_grip.text: Your pattern is real but your hands are still mostly on the wheel. Worth understanding, not worth panicking over.

steady_pull.label: Steady pull
steady_pull.text: There's a working loop here — it has triggers, a schedule, and a job. Loops like this respond well to being understood and redesigned.

deep_loop.label: Deep loop
deep_loop.text: This loop is carrying real weight and collecting real costs. That's not a character flaw — it's a well-built cycle, and it deserves real support, not another self-discipline plan. Talking to someone who treats this is a strength move.

noDominantLoop.title: No dominant loop
noDominantLoop.read: Your answers don't point to one strong pattern — either your use really is mostly intentional, or your pattern is subtler than a few minutes of questions can catch. Both are legitimate results, and forcing a label would be exactly the kind of fake precision we promised not to do.
